text: A server can arrive in the CMDB from three different places -- Discovery, an import from an asset tool, or a technician's manual entry. Nothing tells the CMDB that any two of those might actually describe the same real machine unless a rule tells it how to recognize a match. That's the job of an Identification Rule, and it's the single biggest lever on your duplicate rate, which is exactly what the previous lesson's dashboard score measures.

A weak rule matches on Name alone, but a display label like WEB-PROD-01 is just something a human typed, not a stable identifier. A real identification rule for a server CI class defines an independent identifier, reliable enough on its own, like a hardware serial number, plus one or more dependent identifiers that only prove a match in combination -- Host Name together with Domain, for instance, since a hostname alone isn't unique across domains but the pair usually is. Get this rule right, and the same server reported by two different sources lands on one record. Get it wrong, and it lands on two.

Identification and Reconciliation solve two completely different problems, and the two get conflated constantly. Identification decides whether two incoming records are the same CI in the first place. Reconciliation decides, once they've already been confirmed to be the same CI, which source's value should win when two sources disagree about a specific field on that record.

Discovery might report OS version 2022 on a Windows server, while a manual CSV import done six months ago still says 2019. Without a reconciliation rule, the dangerous default is whichever source happened to write most recently wins, letting a stale manual import silently overwrite a correct, freshly discovered value, or the reverse. A well-implemented CMDB avoids that by designating, per field rather than per CI class, which source is authoritative -- Discovery for OS version, since it inspects the actual running machine, but a manual entry or asset-system feed for something like Business Owner or Cost Center, which Discovery simply can't observe at all.

Loose or missing Identification Rules are the leading real-world cause of duplicate CIs, which the next lesson tackles head-on. Missing Reconciliation Rules are a leading cause of correct data getting silently overwritten by bad data. Together, these two rule types are the actual mechanism sitting behind two of the Health Dashboard's four scored dimensions from the last lesson -- Compliance and duplicate rate.
